title: 7 Christmas Light Mistakes That Make Your Living Room Look CHEAP

scenes.text: Sweetheart, I've noticed something. The houses that feel the coziest at Christmas don't have the most decorations. They have the best light. Soft, warm, low light, coming from a dozen little places around the room. And the houses that feel cold and cheap almost always have one big bright light on the ceiling, blazing down like a hospital waiting room.
scenes.query: cozy living room Christmas lights warm
scenes.caption: THE BEST LIGHT

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you seven Christmas lighting mistakes that make a living room look cheap, and the simple fixes, most of them free. And stay with me, because the last one is the trick my mother used on Christmas Eve, and it turns any room into a Christmas card in about two minutes.
scenes.caption: SEVEN LIGHTING MISTAKES

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty, our little house on Elm Street had one lamp in the front room, an overhead light, and the Christmas tree. That's all. But on Christmas Eve, my mother turned off the overhead light, lit the tree, put a candle in each window, and lit two oil lamps from Grandma Pearl's farm. And the whole room turned gold.
scenes.caption: THE ROOM TURNED GOLD

scenes.text: My father sat in his chair with his pipe, Danny and I lay on the rug under the tree, and the radio played carols, low. Nobody said much. We just sat in that warm light. Seventy-five years later, I can still see it with my eyes closed. In a minute I'll tell you the first mistake, and it's the light on your ceiling.
scenes.caption: I CAN STILL SEE IT

scenes.text: Mistake number one. Using the overhead light. A big light in the middle of the ceiling throws hard shadows, makes everybody look tired, and flattens all your beautiful decorations. At Christmas, turn it off, and leave it off after supper. Light the room from low places instead, at the height of a table or lower. That's how candlelight and firelight work, and that's why they feel cozy.
scenes.caption: TURN IT OFF

scenes.text: Decorators call it layers of light, honey. A table lamp in one corner, a floor lamp in another, the tree, some candles, a little string of lights on a shelf. Five or six small lights, at different heights, all around the room. No dark corners, and no bright spots. If you only remember one thing tonight, remember that.
scenes.query: table lamp floor lamp tree corners
scenes.caption: LAYERS OF LIGHT

scenes.text: Mistake number two. Cold white light bulbs. Many of the new bulbs give off a bluish white light, like a store or an office. Look on the box for the word warm white, or the number twenty-seven hundred. That's the color of an old-fashioned bulb, soft and golden. Put warm bulbs in every lamp in the living room for December. It costs a few dollars and changes the whole room.
scenes.caption: TWENTY-SEVEN HUNDRED

scenes.text: And the same for the Christmas lights on the tree, sweetheart. Warm white, not cool white. Cool white lights look blue and icy, like a freezer case. If you like colored lights, the old-fashioned soft colors look warmer than the bright neon ones. My grandson bought blue lights one year, and his wife said the living room looked like a swimming pool.
scenes.caption: LIKE A SWIMMING POOL

scenes.text: Mistake number three. All the lights on the tree, and nowhere else. The tree glows in the corner, and the rest of the room sits in the dark. Spread a little light around. A string of small lights tucked in the garland on the mantel. A few in a glass jar on a bookshelf. A string around a mirror. A little lit tree in the kitchen window.
scenes.query: fairy lights in glass jar shelf
scenes.caption: SPREAD IT AROUND

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. And a tip for those little lights in jars and bowls. Buy the tiny battery strings with the thin copper wire, the ones they call fairy lights. They cost about two dollars, they have a timer, and the wire disappears. Tuck them in a bowl of pinecones or ornaments. It glows like magic.
scenes.caption: IT GLOWS LIKE MAGIC

scenes.text: Mistake number four. Too few lights on the tree. People put one string on a seven-foot tree, and it looks thin and spotty. The old rule is one hundred lights for every foot of tree. A seven-foot tree needs about seven hundred lights. That sounds like a lot, honey, but that's what makes a tree glow from the inside, instead of looking like it has a few freckles.
scenes.caption: A HUNDRED PER FOOT
scenes.chapter: 4. Not enough lights on the tree

scenes.text: And put them on the right way. Don't just wrap them around the outside like a bandage. Start at the trunk at the bottom, and run the lights out along each big branch to the tip, and back in to the trunk, then on to the next branch. It takes an hour longer, but the lights go deep into the tree, and it glows from the middle out.
scenes.caption: DEEP INTO THE TREE

scenes.text: And here's a little trick for an old tree, honey, or a skinny fake one. Put a second string of lights deep inside, right against the trunk, all the way up. It lights the tree from the center, so you can't see the gaps between the branches anymore. The whole tree looks fuller and richer, like it cost twice as much. My daughter-in-law's fake tree is thirty years old, and nobody knows.
scenes.caption: LIGHT THE TRUNK

scenes.text: So far, the ceiling light off, warm bulbs, lights spread around the room, and plenty of lights deep in the tree. Now mistake number five. Blinking, chasing, flashing lights inside the house. My father always said blinking lights belong on a fire truck. They make a room feel busy and nervous. Set every string to steady. Steady light is calm, and calm is cozy.
scenes.caption: STEADY IS CALM

scenes.text: Mistake number six. Cords everywhere. A tangle of green and white wires running across the floor and down the wall to the outlet. It looks messy, and it's dangerous. Run the cords along the back of the furniture and behind the tree skirt. Use a cord cover, or tape them under the edge of the rug. And use battery lights wherever you can, so there's no cord at all.
scenes.caption: HIDE THE CORDS

scenes.text: And be safe, sweetheart. Never run cords under a rug where people walk, because they can wear through and start a fire. Don't plug too many strings into one outlet. Use a power strip with a switch, or a timer, so everything goes off at bedtime. And keep the tree watered every day. A dry tree and hot lights is how Christmas fires start.
scenes.caption: SAFETY FIRST

scenes.text: And now mistake number seven, the trick I promised. Forgetting the candles. Nothing in the world makes a room feel like Christmas the way candlelight does. My mother's trick on Christmas Eve was simple. Turn off every lamp in the house, except the tree. Then light candles. In the windows, on the table, on the mantel. Then sit down, and let your eyes adjust.
scenes.caption: TURN OFF EVERY LAMP

scenes.text: In two minutes, honey, the room changes. Everybody's face looks soft and young. The ornaments sparkle. The children get quiet. That's the Christmas card I promised. And today, use the good battery candles with a flickering flame, especially around children, pets and greenery. Put them in glass holders or lanterns. Nobody can tell the difference across the room.
scenes.caption: EVERYBODY LOOKS YOUNG

scenes.text: If you do use real candles, keep them on a plate or in a tall glass holder, well away from the tree, the curtains and the garland. Never leave them burning when you leave the room, or when you go to bed. My mother kept a little brass snuffer by every candle, and the last job of Christmas Eve was mine. Snuffing out the candles, one by one.
scenes.caption: ONE BY ONE

scenes.text: And one more kind of light, sweetheart. The fireplace. If you have one, use it on Christmas Eve. If you don't, there's no shame in a little tabletop lantern, or a row of candles in the empty fireplace, or even the fireplace video on the television with the sound turned low. My grandchildren insist on the television fire every year. They say it's tradition. It's been on since two thousand nine.
scenes.caption: THE FIREPLACE

scenes.text: And don't forget the windows, sweetheart, because that's what people see from the street. A single candle in every window, the old American way, on a timer from dusk to bedtime. In colonial days, a candle in the window meant a traveler was welcome. My mother kept one burning in our front window every night in December, for my uncle Ray, who was overseas in nineteen fifty-two.
scenes.caption: A TRAVELER IS WELCOME

scenes.text: He came home that Christmas, honey, the day before Christmas Eve, on the afternoon train. He walked up Elm Street in his uniform, and the first thing he said when he came through the door was, I saw the candle from the corner. My mother put her face in her apron and didn't say anything for a long time.
scenes.caption: I SAW THE CANDLE

scenes.text: So one more time. Turn off the ceiling light. Warm white bulbs in every lamp. Layers of light, five or six small ones, all around the room. A hundred lights for every foot of tree, deep in the branches. Steady, never blinking. Hide the cords. And candles, in the windows and on the table. That's how my mother turned our little front room gold every Christmas Eve.
scenes.caption: THE ROOM TURNED GOLD

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. White lights or colored lights on your tree? And do you leave a candle in the window? The whole playlist of Grandma's Christmas tips is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: WHITE OR COLORED?
